nameStory: The primrose moth gets its name from its intimate relationship with evening primrose flowers, where it spends its entire life cycle. Adults rest inside the pale yellow blooms during the day, while their caterpillars develop by feeding exclusively on the flower buds of these same plants. It's a perfect match of pink and yellow colors that mirrors the soft hues of primrose petals.
description: The primrose moth is a delicate nocturnal moth with a wingspan of about 30mm (roughly 1.2 inches). Its most striking feature is the beautiful pink and pale yellow color combination - a rosy pink head and forewings decorated with creamy yellow markings, paired with a pale yellow thorax and creamy white hindwings and abdomen. This small moth belongs to the cutworm moth family (Noctuidae), though unlike many of its relatives, it's a specialist that feeds only on evening primrose plants. You'll find adults flying at night during summer months, perfectly timed to match when their host plants are blooming.

idTips.label: Pink and yellow coloring
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive pink head and forewings with pale yellow or creamy markings - this color combination is quite unique among New England moths

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: With a wingspan of about 30mm, this moth is roughly the size of a large butterfly or small to medium moth - smaller than a sphinx moth but larger than many micro-moths

idTips.label: Evening primrose association
idTips.description: Often found resting inside or near evening primrose flowers during the day - the moth's colors blend beautifully with the pale yellow petals

idTips.label: Creamy white hindwings
idTips.description: The hindwings are pale creamy white, creating a nice contrast with the pink forewings when the wings are spread

idTips.label: Nocturnal behavior
idTips.description: Active at night and attracted to lights, but during the day you might spot them tucked into evening primrose blooms looking almost like part of the flower

habitat: Look for primrose moths in areas where evening primroses grow - typically disturbed soils, roadsides, old fields, meadow edges, and waste areas throughout New England. These plants prefer well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and full sun exposure. The moths will be found wherever their host plants bloom, from sea level to moderate elevations in both rural and suburban settings.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet - larvae are developing underground after overwintering as pupae in the soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time for adults, usually coinciding with evening primrose blooming from June through August. Look for them at flowers during the day or flying at night.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down as evening primroses finish blooming. New eggs have been laid and are developing into larvae that will feed on remaining flower buds.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity - moths overwinter as pupae buried in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger their transformation into adults.

funFact: Primrose moths are such devoted flower specialists that they've evolved to be perfectly camouflaged alarm clocks - the adults emerge from underground pupation precisely timed to match when evening primrose buds are developing, even adjusting their internal clocks to local flowering schedules that can vary by weeks across different locations!
confusionNotes: The pink and yellow coloration is quite distinctive, but you might confuse primrose moths with some pink-tinged cutworm moths. The key difference is habitat - if you're not near evening primroses, you're probably looking at a different species. Remember: 'Pink near primroses = primrose moth.'
compareHints: The closely related Arcigera Flower Moth (Schinia arcigera) is the most similar species in the same genus found in New England. While both are flower specialists with similar sizes, the Arcigera Flower Moth typically has more muted coloring and associates with different host plants in the aster family rather than evening primroses. The primrose moth's bright pink and yellow combination is more vibrant and distinctive than its cousin's more subdued tones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Primrose Moth (Schinia florida) is very similar but feeds on evening primroses instead of asters - if you find small flower moths around yellow evening primrose blooms rather than purple/white aster flowers, you've likely found the primrose species instead.
